lead.t: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a group of inter‑related inflammatory rheumatic diseases that primarily affect the axial skeleton (sacroiliac joints and spine) and may involve peripheral joints, entheses, skin, eyes and the gastrointestinal tract.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with 6 months of morning stiffness and heel pain; X‑ray is normal. What is the next diagnostic step — MRI of sacroiliac joints to detect early sacroiliitis.
How does you differentiate axial SpA from mechanical low back pain on history — inflammatory back pain improves with activity and has night stiffness >30 min.
A patient on a TNF inhibitor develops fever and cough; what must you rule out before continuing therapy — active tuberculosis, using chest X‑ray and sputum test.
Why are NSAIDs preferred as first‑line over steroids in SpA — they target prostaglandin‑mediated inflammation without systemic immunosuppression and have better safety in chronic use.
What extra‑articular manifestation should you screen for in all SpA patients — anterior uveitis, examined by slit‑lamp.
Explain why a patient with severe spinal fusion may develop restrictive lung disease — loss of thoracic spine mobility limits chest expansion, reducing vital capacity.
In a low‑resource setting without MRI, how can you still diagnose axial SpA — rely on ASAS clinical criteria plus pelvic X‑ray showing sacroiliitis.
What is the rationale for physiotherapy in SpA and a key component of the program — maintain posture and chest expansion; daily spinal stretching is essential.
ai.title: Spondyloarthritis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a family of inflammatory diseases affecting the spine, sacroiliac joints and entheses, often with skin, eye or gut involvement. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, imaging and HLA‑B27, with severity staged by functional limitation and radiographic damage.

b: Axial SpA: sacroiliitis on X‑ray or MRI + ≥1 SpA feature
Peripheral SpA: arthritis, enthesitis or dactylitis + ≥1 SpA feature
sections.p: SpA comprises axial and peripheral forms that share inflammation of entheses and a strong association with HLA‑B27. Diagnosis uses the ASAS criteria: back pain >3 months, age <45, plus imaging or HLA‑B27 plus clinical features.

b: Mild: BASFI <3, no radiographic fusion
Moderate: BASFI 3‑5, early syndesmophytes
Severe: BASFI >5, extensive fusion, reduced vital capacity
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional indices (BASFI) and radiographic progression (modified Stoke Ankylosing Spondylitis Spinal Score). Advanced disease shows syndesmophytes and limited chest expansion.

b: Genetic: HLA‑B27 positivity
Infection‑triggered reactive arthritis (GI or GU infections, TB, HIV)
Associated skin disease (psoriasis) or IBD
sections.p: SpA is not infectious; it is immune‑mediated with a strong genetic predisposition (HLA‑B27). In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections (TB, HIV) can trigger reactive arthritis.

b: Inflammatory back pain: night pain, improves with activity
Enthesitis: heel pain at Achilles insertion
Dactylitis: sausage‑shaped digit swelling
sections.p: Patients report insidious inflammatory back pain that improves with exercise, morning stiffness >30 min, and peripheral enthesitis. Extra‑articular features include uveitis, psoriasis and diarrhoea.
Use tests that answer specific clinical questions; when imaging is unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and simple labs.

t.b: Is sacroiliitis present? Bilateral grade ≥2 changes confirm axial SpA.
Detect active inflammation when X‑ray is normal; bone‑marrow oedema indicates early disease.
Supports diagnosis; positive result raises pre‑test probability but is not definitive.
Are inflammatory markers elevated? High levels suggest active disease and guide treatment intensity.
Is anterior uveitis present? Confirms extra‑articular involvement.

b: Progressive spinal fusion causing restrictive lung disease
Fracture through ankylosed spine after minor trauma
Anterior uveitis threatening vision
sections.p: Complications arise from chronic inflammation and reduced chest expansion, leading to respiratory compromise and spinal fractures.

b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) – first‑line for pain and stiffness; avoid in active peptic ulcer or severe renal disease
TNF‑α inhibitors (e.g., etanercept) – for NSAID‑refractory disease; avoid in active infection or TB without prophylaxis
IL‑17 inhibitors (e.g., secukinumab) – alternative when TNF blockers fail; caution in candidiasis
Physiotherapy: daily stretching, posture training, breathing exercises
sections.p: Treat inflammation first, then address function and comorbidities. Use NSAIDs, then biologic agents if disease remains active. Physical therapy is essential.

b: Assess BASFI and chest expansion every 6‑12 months
Screen for TB before biologics; repeat annually if risk persists
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus
sections.p: Regular monitoring of function, spinal mobility and drug safety prevents irreversible damage.

b: Rheumatoid arthritis – symmetrical peripheral joints, no sacroiliitis
Degenerative disc disease – pain worsens with activity, no HLA‑B27 association
Infective spondylodiscitis – fever, elevated CRP, positive cultures
sections.p: Conditions that cause back pain or enthesitis may mimic SpA.

b: Normal CRP/ESR does not exclude active SpA
Negative HLA‑B27 does not rule out disease, especially in non‑white populations
sections.p: Certain tests may be normal despite active disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision (possible uveitis complication)
Severe chest pain with dyspnoea (possible spinal fracture or cardiac involvement)
Rapidly worsening back pain with fever (suspect infection)
